headline: Komoru is from Old Japanese 隠る (komoru), and its stem relates to “fill, filling”, so it is likely cognate with 込む (komu, “to be crowded, be packed”).

headline: キャリア is from English career, though its pitch accent suggests English carrier.

sources.quote: From English career. The use of キャ for transcription here is rather peculiar given that it is typically used for the English sequence /kæ/ which is absent in the original English pronunciation. The pitch accent also somewhat indicates that this transcription is more suitable for English carrier, though Japanese pitch accent isn't known for consistently corresponding to English stress.

headline: パチンコ appears from the Taishō period, a compound of ぱちん (pachin, onomatopoeia for a small hard thing striking something else) plus 子 (-ko).

sources.quote: Appears from the Taishō period in the early 1900s.
Compound of ぱちん (pachin, onomatopoeia for a small hard thing striking something else; compare English kaching) + 子 (-ko, suffix used to form nouns, often diminutive).
A pinball-like children's game was first called ガチャンコ (gachanko) of similar derivation, with this more gambling-oriented machine becoming popular from around 1947.

headline: Sasageru is from Old Japanese 捧ぐ (sasagu), a contraction of 差し上ぐ (sasiagu), whence modern 差し上げる (sashiageru).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese verb 捧ぐ (sasagu), a contraction of 差し上ぐ (sasiagu), whence also modern Japanese 差し上げる (sashiageru).
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

headline: Nagisa is from Old Japanese, possibly 凪ぎ (nagi, “calming, dying down”) plus 磯 (sa, “rocky shore, pebble beach”).

sources.quote: ⟨naɡi₁sa⟩ → */naɡʲisa/ → /naɡisa/
From Old Japanese.

Possibly a compound of 凪(な)ぎ (nagi, “calming, dying down”, the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 凪(な)ぐ (nagu, “to calm down, to die down”, as of waves or wind), cognate with 和(なご)やか (nagoyaka, “calm, quiet”)) + 磯(さ) (sa, “rocky shore, pebble beach”), where sa is an ancient alternative for so, the abbreviated combining reading of modern 磯(いそ) (iso), cognate with 石(いし) (ishi, “rock, stone”).

headline: Kurōto is 玄 (kuro, “deep, profound”) plus 人 (-uto, “person”), an old root form of 人 (hito).

sources.quote: */kuroputo/ → */kurofuto/ → /kurouto/
Compound of 玄(くろ) (kuro, “deep, profound”) + 人(うと) (-uto, “person”).

The term 人 (hito, “person”) appears in various older compounds with a root form of 人 (*puto → *buto → *udo, *puto → *futo → *uto). This form is never seen in isolation, and it often undergoes further phonetic changes to combine with preceding vowels. Compare the formation of 仲人 (nakōdo), from naka + udo; 旅人 (tabiudo), from tabi + udo; 素人 (shirōto), from shiro + uto.
